title: Appreciating Tathata
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett invites listeners to cultivate an appreciation for reality as it is, without judgment or attachment, by embracing the present moment with openness and softness. This approach allows us to experience life's beauty and majesty without striving for specific outcomes, and instead, trusts in the unfolding of life itself. By doing so, we can connect more deeply with ourselves and others, and find a sense of freedom and peace that arises from being fully present.

sentences.text: Good afternoon, everybody.
Well, I really appreciated Norman's and Kate's talks, didn't you?
So moving and important for us.
I don't remember most of what they said, but that's okay.
But it's very important to somehow bring forward together these different ways of being a person in a world.
I was especially moved by the way Kate started out with thank yous, and I'm tempted to do that, but then I realized that if I did, we wouldn't have any time for the talk.
So I'll just generally say thank you.
That's what I'll do for now.
Thank you so much.
This style of practice is so family-based, community-based.
We learned everything we learned from each other, don't you think?
So I'm grateful for that.
A great advantage of sitting on my butt in the library all retreat is that I'm next to all these interesting-looking books.
There are treasures in there.
It reminds me of the value of happenstance and browsing and having time to just look around.
So much of my time is more directive, and I have the privilege of being on the internet, where I can pick and choose anything I want.
So this felt like the books were choosing me, in between people.
I get a little distracted.
I ran into a lovely little volume of poetry, a slim volume with a blurry image of somebody walking along a Himalayan trail.
So I picked that up.
It turned out to be a little book of poems and short essays by a Tibetan refugee, somebody named Tenzin Tsundue.
It appears to have been self-published by his brother in a limited edition printed in India.
On the inside it says it cost 50 rupees.
How this little book came to be sitting in our library, I don't know.
It must have been donated by somebody who went to India.
I was holding this little book and thinking about how powerful objects are.
We live in a material world, we think.
And if we look deeply into any object, there's such gravity to it.
It's amazing.
How could this book be here, created by these people, expressing something, in my hands now?
The feeling of it, the weight of it, the existence of it.
Maybe the uniqueness and surprise of this particular book helped me experience this feeling of amazement, this feeling of connection.
Maybe that's easier for my habitual mind than if it were just another trade paperback from Shambhala Press.
Hundreds of those.
Maybe there are only ten of these in the world.
We don't know.
There's a sort of bottomless somethingness to everything, a kind of is-ness.
Somehow this little book reminded me of that.
That this is.
That this little book is.
That we are.
That this place is.
That the sun came up and went down.
That all of this is.
It's incredible.
And of course everything is that way, not just the things that our senses point out to us or get interested in.
And not just material things either.
Everything.
Even the things that we think are ordinary or unlikable or even disgusting.
Things we think shouldn't be here.
If we pay attention and notice, I think they all have this quality of, oh.
So anyway, here's a poem by Tenzin Tsundue, strangely called "Space Bar of Proposal."
*Pull your ceiling halfway down and you can create a mezzanine for me.
Your walls open into cupboards.
Is there an empty shelf for me?
Let me grow in your garden with your roses and prickly pears.
I'll sleep under your bed and watch TV in the mirror.
Do you have an ear on your balcony?
I'm singing from your window.*
*Open your door.
Let me in.
I am resting on your doorstep.
Call me when you are awake.
I'm resting on your doorstep.
Call me when you are awake.*
I love that image of sleeping under the bed, watching TV in the mirror.
Some people have fears of monsters under the bed when they're growing up.
How about a sweet Tibetan refugee?
Call me when you're awake.
So that's really what the Buddha is offering too, isn't it?
Call me when you're awake.
I'm here.
I've been practicing with you all along.
I'm ready to support you in entering this life fully.
And don't worry, says the Buddha on the doorstep or under the bed, I don't mind if you don't notice the invitation.
I won't be offended if you're too busy or not ready.
I'll just wait till you're ready to really enter your life.
But then, entering our life isn't quite right, is it?
That would mean we're somehow outside our life.
How can we be outside of our own life?
Maybe the Buddha calls on us to appreciate the full lifeness of our life.
The completeness, the is-ness, the okay-ness of our life.
We don't really have good language for this.
And the language we do have is so good at talking us the other direction, talking us out of any kind of appreciation for our life.
What are you talking about, appreciate my life?
I have too many problems.
I'm too unworthy.
So it's been such a privilege to get to sit in the Dokusan room.
And I do pay attention to the people, not the books, when they're there.
I'm never bored, though.
And you know what the most common theme is?
The most common theme is, I don't think I'm good enough.
Which Norman also brought up this morning.
So that seems to be what our language is so good at telling us: the ways that we're not good enough.
So maybe the Buddha resting on the doorstep is ready to call for you in a different language than that.
A language of presence.
A language of deep seeing.
A language of interconnection.
But none of this is quite right.
A language beyond the limits of language.
Our language is so good at this and that.
Skills, tasks, results, failures, successes, me and you, them and us.
Our whole political sphere seems to be built in this kind of language too.
Tomorrow, yesterday, should and shouldn't.
So maybe we also need another kind of language.
A language of fundamental appreciation.
A language that doesn't allow us to convince ourselves we aren't good enough, because that doesn't make any sense in this language.
There's no way to say that in that language.
How can there be not good enough?
The Buddhists have been pondering this for a while, so let's look at their language.
There is a Buddhist term that's helpful, I think.
And again, I think Norman probably mentioned this yesterday.
A kind of language for the this-ness of things.
The is-ness of things.
The as-they-are-ness of things.
In Sanskrit it's tathata.
Tathata.
It's usually translated in English as thus-ness or such-ness.
The root of this word is just a Sanskrit word for thus, just like in English, thus.
One Buddhist studies scholar wrote, "We know we're experiencing the thus-ness of reality when we experience something and say to ourselves, 'Yes, that's it.
That's the way things are.'" You know that feeling?
Yeah, that's it.
It's usually like we already kind of knew that, right?
It doesn't make sense in another way of thinking, but there's a feeling to that.
Yeah, that's it.
That's how it is.
An appreciation of this such-ness, to use that word provisionally, really helps us.
It drops us into a felt sense of the majesty, the beauty, the fragility, the unbelievable improbability of everything.
How could it be that from the infinite causes and conditions and possible chains of events, going back billions of years to the Big Bang, we have this?
Why would it be this?
Why would it be this?
It's amazing.
I was reading another scholar who was critical of the use of the word such-ness, because, he was saying, that implies a kind of solidification, a ratification, like there's a something that's such.
Of course, it's really more fluid than that.
This other person suggested "being such," just being such, as a way to talk about this idea, which isn't really an idea either.

It's a deep practice of softening around this powerful pattern of dividing everything up, making it so concrete, right and wrong, outcomes, results, and we open our hearts to an open-endedness, to an openness, to an aliveness, just being such, just this.
I think a lot about the improbability of all this and the amazing such-ness of this whenever we're here practicing, especially at these retreats.
Things that aren't unlikely: this, like actually this.
How did all this happen?
Of course, we all have stories about how this happened.

I was at such-and-such a place, and I met this person, and they said this, or I ran into this book in the bookstore or the library, or I was in crisis, and my friend said that, and I tried this, and boy, it really helped.
We do like our stories, but I think we know there's a lot more to it than our story, that reality can't be explained in narrative, which isn't a problem.
There are wonderful stories.

But I think it helps us touch the such-ness, the is-ness of things, to remember, and these retreats help us remember this so radically, that our stories are just stories, and after a while they just fall away like leaves from an autumn tree.
So I was remembering one of my favorite stories about all this, in which Norman is a protagonist.
I don't know why you would remember this, but it's maybe very early, January.

Yeah, it was January of 1988, and I'm 21 years old, or just turned 22, and I had been at Green Gulch Farm Zen Center for a couple of months, trying the Zen thing out, which was interesting and difficult.
The metaphor that kept coming to me at the time was that this is like trying on a different kind of set of clothes, and I kind of like them, I don't know if they really fit, you know?
And I was preparing, I thought, to go somewhere, traveling or back to college, I don't remember, but it must have been in December, actually.
It was the last meal that I was going to be there.
It was lunch.

And I'm waiting in line in front of the lunch serve-up at Green Gulch in the dining room, and the director of Green Gulch is standing behind me, named Norman Fischer, and he taps me on the shoulder and says, "Excuse me, would you like to stay here and work in the kitchen?"
And I said, "Okay."
So then I stayed another four or five months.
And then, part B of the story: I went to the first staff meeting, so now I'm suddenly on staff.
That was the entire interview, hiring, and discernment process.
I'm at the first staff meeting, and somebody hands me a form and explains to me, oh, this is a new form that we have for staff.
We want you to pick a practice leader and work with that practice leader and make a practice plan.
I didn't really say it out loud, but the implication was, you young students tend to just come here and goof off.
You get a free place to live, a hundred bucks a month, and we never see you in the Zendos.
We want a little more control than that.
And I'm sitting next to a woman monastic, a female monastic named Fu Schroeder.

As I'm puzzling over this form, because I had to tick off a bunch of boxes with people's names on them, or maybe a blank, I forget, and I had to write down or tick off the name of a practice leader, I didn't know who to put down.
I'd only been there a couple of months.
And Fu whispers to me, "He's really easy."
So, 30 years later, here we are.
Enjoy that story.
That might have actually happened.
So it's amazing, isn't it, the suchness of each moment, sitting in the Zendo built by our own hands from a ruined church social hall.
Each of us somehow lining up our lives to show up here this weekend, doing our practice in the way that we each do it.
Many of us getting to do this together for decades, and watching the way we each do it change and morph, and annoyingly not change enough.
Watching our love for each other grow, and our patterns of reactivity, and seeing how it's all just so much stuff in the mind.
I so appreciated Norman's bringing up Dr.

Wright's model of three levels of consciousness, how we move back and forth together between all three of those: experiencing each other directly, experiencing our thoughts and opinions and excitements and judgments about each other, and experiencing our sense of who we are together in the mind and in the heart.
And sesshin, this particular way of practicing, is such a great support for the appreciation, for the practice of suchness.
This complex, rich, long weekend we're having, we call sesshin.
Sesshin is a compound word in Sino-Japanese.
Confusingly, there's modern Japanese, and there's the way Japanese people pronounce Chinese characters that they're borrowing for religion.
It's kind of like the high Latin of Japanese.
So this is the latter.
Just to warn you, if you go to Japan sometime and start spouting these Japanese terms you think you know, they won't understand you, because they don't talk that way, actually.
I read a little piece by Natalie Goldberg.
Do you know who she is?
Wonderful Zen writing teacher.

She wrote a little piece, I don't know how long ago this was, about going to Japan and excitedly chanting the robe chant that we chant early in the morning, which is also in this kind of Sino-Japanese dialect.
And her host was like, what are you talking about?
It's just gobbledygook.
It doesn't make any sense.
So anyway, sesshin is in that branch of Japanese.
Two words together.
The first is setsu, which gets condensed into sess.
But setsu means to touch, to be in contact with.
And shin is the word for heart, mind.
Same character.
It's a beautiful little swooping character, too.
Lovely.
The same character means heart, the same character means mind.
So that's according to the title of our event, the direction, the invitation: to touch the heart, mind.
To touch the heart, mind.
So, noticing what the title is not: it's not improve shin.
It's not fix shin.
It's not what's wrong with me, shin.
It's touch shin.
So that's all we have to do.
It's just touch it.
Just be in contact.
Just suchness.
This character *shin* is in a lot of our treasured texts.
We chanted it many times early this morning.
And it's also on Kate's new rakusu.
Did you know Kate has a new rakusu?
Many of you helped us sew it.
We created a shuso rakusu for Kate.
On the back we put, in big characters in the middle, the character for open, and this character *shin*.
So: opening the heart-mind.
Don't you think that's what she's doing and helping us to do?
Then on one side we put the characters for shuso.
On the other side we put her name, which is Ru Shin, dragon heart-mind.
So the dragon heart-mind is helping us open the heart-mind, shuso.
Somewhere along the line, heart and mind got separated.
So *shin* helps us invite them, allow them to merge back together.
Maybe they were never really apart anyway.
Another trick of language and mind.

Sesshin is our take on the Japanese monastic practice of life in the sodo, life in the monk's hall, in which, not forever, but for a year or three, the monks sit and sleep and live at their place in the zendo, in the monk's hall.
It's a little bit deeper than our seats, so they have room to lie down, but that's your spot.
It's like one tatami mat, like we have in the back room.
There's a little wood cupboard at the end, where you can roll up your futon and your blanket and put your toothbrush, your razor maybe.
Not room for a whole lot of other stuff.
I'm sure there are very strict rules about what you can keep in there, but there are other good rules.
So we're enacting that kind of life for a couple of days.
A life in which we just stay in our spot, trust and place our whole heart and our whole body in our spot.
We don't choose our spot, we just stay there.
And it's wonderful that we're being served meals right there in our spot, this sesshin.
The suchness of that is off the charts, you know?
How did we pull that off?
These elaborate three-bowl meals cooked in...
Have you looked at our kitchen?
People wouldn't cook for one in that kitchen.
Yeah, we cook for 30.
And the beautiful job the servers are doing, coordinated by their [unclear: "soku"], really.
Wow.
But what I love about that is not that we pulled it off, oh, good for us.
Oh, that's fun.
It's just another support for this radical practice of just being, just receiving.
We don't get to choose the food, we don't go get it, it just appears as normal, just there it is in our bowl.
That way of living is the Japanese take, through Dogen and his teachers and colleagues, on the life of the Buddha and his monks and nuns.
They'd get up early every morning to meditate, usually camped out on the edge of a town, some field somewhere, maybe under some trees.
Then after a few hours of meditation, everybody walks into the town with their begging bowls held out quietly, going from door to door, receiving their food just like we're receiving our food.
And that in itself is a very rich practice.
It's not just going to the grocery store.
It's a deep interaction with their hearts and with the people in the town.
There are quite a few teachings and sutras about stuff that happens and things they learn from it, going on their alms round.
We won't go into that, but it's really fascinating.
The Buddha really saw that as an opportunity for training.
Then they walk back mindfully to their camp.
I read in one of the commentaries that some of them took on the practice of mindful walking so sincerely that if they took a single step without mindfulness of walking, they'd go back and start over.
So for some of them, it was a long time before they got back.
For me, that would be on the way there.
They had to get back in time because they needed to eat their one big meal a day and be all done by midday.
That was the rule, because the Buddha wanted to create a simple life, a quiet life, a life with just tremendous space for practice.
So they'd eat their meal, the Buddha would give a dharma talk, and then individual practice for the rest of the afternoon and into the night.
Maybe meeting with a senior monastic if you have a question about your practice.
Maybe a few camp chores.
Maybe attending to the sick monks or nuns, and they'd set up little shelters for them to keep the rain off them.
But basically just quietly practicing every day, day after day.
No days off.
No days off.
So that's the lovely point about the Buddha's practice.
His awakening, he was about, I forget, about 30 years old.
He lived another 40-something years.
Just every day, every day practicing.
It wasn't in his language, probably, like, "I'm tired of this.
I'm going to take a day off, you know, and kick back."
Because what is there to do but be alive?
And what is this practice but an expression of that?
So what a rich field of practice it is in our sesshin.
Maybe it's nice to hear these stories and remind ourselves when we get discouraged.
Which we will, of course.
That we're holding a long thread going back a long ways in a lot of cultures and places.
We're tending a certain kind of light.
Like Dogen said at the end of our text, who would take, for me that's a different text, but Dogen said:
*Who would take wasteful delight in the spark from the Flintstone?*
So we're keeping something going here.
And what a relief it can be when from time to time the busyness of that second reflective consciousness settles for a moment.
And we can just see the play of the light on the floor.
Hear the cars going by or a bird.
Or even notice a thought.
It's just a thought.
Nothing to be too excited about.
Dropping into this orientation of experiencing.
Of being.
But it's not like there's anything wrong with this second level of consciousness.
This is part of our life and so a part of us.
And we are complete as we are.
But maybe we get a little out of balance.
A little out of whack.
So this practice of privileging experiencing for some days, maybe this can help us in our relationship to our busy minds.
Not to get rid of them or to solve them or fix them, but to experience it.
To just experience it.
Oh, that is one compelling thought.
Damn.
Or, that is one silly thought.
What the heck?
What is this head full of mush?
What's that about?
Just there it is.
And there it is.
And there it is.
And no matter what grabs a hold of us, isn't it wonderful?
Isn't it so encouraging to notice that we can come back?
That we can always return.
It's always available to us.
Sometimes it takes a while.
But it's always possible to come back to this feeling.
Breath.
Body.
Contact with the earth.
This moment.
This life.
So maybe an appreciation for the suchness of things is kind of like when our second consciousness just calms down enough so that all three are in harmony.
All three are in a healthy relationship.
There's an experience of what's happening.
Wonderful.
There's some reflective elaboration in that experience.
Aren't we lucky to have these big brains, you know?
Cool.
And there's some concept of self that emerges, an emerging quality of that experience.
And then, and then, we're quiet.
We can watch it all settle back down.
Fade back away into the silence.
No need to hold on to any of it.
The me-ness comes and the me-ness goes.
Inhaling.
Exhaling.
So please, let's make full use of this opportunity.
It's a big effort to put it together, for whatever involvement you had in this.
Just getting here is a big effort.
Arranging everything you had to arrange is a big commitment.
Whoever's minding the store or the kids at home or watching the dog, we can be grateful to and show our appreciation by taking this seriously.
Serious has a weight we don't need to add to it, though.
The suchness serious.
The just-this serious.
The just-being-present serious.
We don't need the ponderous, top-heavy serious so much.
Trusting the silence.
And silence is not a rule against speaking or a prohibition but an opportunity.
An invitation to deep settling.
It's natural to talk less.
So let's keep playing with that.
Maybe we can all be a little quieter.
Not as a pushing down but as an allowing.
As a dropping.
And supporting that with our body.
So it's not just not talking.
Lowering the gaze.
Not looking around so much.
So many little dramas playing out all around us, you know?
Oh wow, did you see that?
So-and-so looked at so-and-so, and then the server did that and then that happened.
Okay.
And then the opinions start, right?
Paying attention to the way we hold the body.
This way of holding the body while walking is so supportive of presence.
The way we hold the body in sitting.
Opening the chest.
Dropping the shoulders.
Gently elongating and softening the spine.
And this silence is an opportunity to pay attention to what kind of effort we're making.
Because we've got a lot more bandwidth, a lot more space to notice.
Can the effort be gentle?
Can the effort be sweet?
Can the feeling of our inner experience be a little more like "ahh," a little less like "I'm going to get through this somehow"?
And all of it is so supported by understanding our retreat weekend as a continuous practice.
As Dogen was trying to tell us in his meditation text that we read this morning.
Just sitting.
Just walking.
No difference.
Just chanting.
Just cooking.
Just cleaning.
Just being here.
The important part is the just.
Just.
Just.
And all this is truly a practice.
We can feel it when our energy starts to get tight.
Something starts bubbling up.
We want to kind of do something.
Notice this and invite it to relax again.
And what's the energy beneath it?
Is it this powerful fear that so many of us seem to carry deep in our hearts that we're not good enough?
And if you think about it, if we all think we're not good enough, who's the one who's good enough that we're comparing ourselves to anyway?
Can our practice of suchness include that too?
Breathing in, recognizing that feeling: not good enough.
Breathing out, releasing that feeling: not good enough.
Breathing in, knowing it's just a story.
Powerful.
Just a story.
Breathing out, knowing it's just a story.
Do we even need these words and concepts?
Just breathing in.
Breathing out.
Breathing in.
Breathing out.
So we're so lucky we get to do this.
We get to do this together.
We may seem to be at times separate, each in our own private Idaho of a little self, but we can feel and touch the feeling of our togetherness.
That's the heart-mind too.
You can really feel it.
And that's how we help each other.
That's how we help each other in sesshin: by feeling deeply.
For this to all work you need a lot of trust.
We need to be able to trust each other.
And I think we need to be able to trust each other really pretty deeply.
So luckily we do trust each other pretty well.
And we can keep growing and watering that trust.
Trusting our shared intention.
Trusting our love for each other.
This is what makes it possible.
Not our self-effort.
It's love.
Maybe that's the best translation in the end for tathata.
Just love.
That's what I wanted to share with you.
Thank you for listening.
But maybe before I give up the seat I'll just say a few words about the ceremony tomorrow with Kate.
Tomorrow, instead of the morning talk, we'll have a fairly significant ceremony called hosenshiki.
We've translated that word as shuso's dharma inquiry ceremony.
It's a ceremony in which our shuso is in the center.
But the center of the matrix of love and sangha.
So she's not on her own.

The pivot part of the ceremony, after various important rituals and movements and chants and preparation, is that each of us has the opportunity to bring forward a dharma question, and the shuso responds.
Each of us a question, shuso each time a response.
These questions are brief and from the heart.
They're expressions of suchness really.
Not so much a technical question or trying to figure out if she's got it, whatever it is.
But what's alive for you?
What's important to you?
And if you're like me and you've always found this kind of Zen question thing really baffling, don't worry about it.
There's a different ceremony in which the transmitted teacher receives the questions.
So now I'm back to being 21 at Green Gulch, and I'm so freaked out by the ceremony.
I felt like, yeah, not good enough.
No way I had a good enough question.
I had this enormous assembly of august dharma geniuses.
I was just a kid.
So I made an arrangement with the teacher to just say, "I don't have a question."
And he'd say, "Thank you," or something.
So anyway, you can trust yourself to say something when the time comes.
And just like we'll trust our shuso, she'll trust herself to respond in some way.
So it doesn't matter if you can't think of a good question.
But you might turn it over a little bit in your mind.
Not too much, but a little bit.
What's important to me now?
What's alive for me now?
In my practice, dharma life.
So that will be tomorrow.
And we'll have some more guests.
We're inviting everyone else who participated in the practice period who may not have been able to come to the sesshin to join us as well.
Just to add more people to our ranks.
I don't think anybody with a question can't ask a question.
We don't need to separate out who gets to ask a question or not.
Okay.
But that's ages from now.
Millennia.
Until then, we have a breath.
We have a breath to breathe.
Wouldn't that be great?
Someone says, "Can you do this, that, or the other thing?"
And you're like, "Oh no, I'm really sorry.
I don't have time.
I have a breath to breathe."
So that's our task.
Thanks a lot.

verbatim.text: Good afternoon everybody. Well, I really appreciated Norman's and Kate's talks, didn't you? So moving and important for us. I don't remember most of what they said, but that's okay. But very important to somehow together bring forward these different ways of being, you know, a person in a world. And I was especially moved by the way Kate started out with thank yous, and so I'm tempted to do that, but then I was just realizing if I did that we wouldn't have any time for the talk. So I'll just generally say thank you. That's what I'll do for now. Thank you so much. This style of practice is so family based, you know, community based. So we learned everything we learned from each other, don't you think? So I'm grateful for that. So a great advantage of being sitting on my butt in the library all retreat is I'm next to all these interesting looking books. There's like treasures in there. Reminds me of the value of happenstance and browsing and having time to just kind of look around. So much of my time is more directive, you know, and I have the privilege of being on the internet and I can just like pick and choose anything I want. So this felt like the books were choosing me in between people. I get a little distracted, you know.

I ran into a lovely little volume of poetry, this little slim volume with an image of kind of a blurry image of somebody walking along in a Himalayan trail. So I picked that up. It turned out to be a little book of poems by a Tibetan refugee. Poems and short essays. Somebody named Tenzin Tsundue appears to have been self-published by his brother in limited edition printed in India. On the inside it says it cost 50 rupees. So how this little book came to be sitting in our library, I don't know. That's been donated by somebody who went to India. And I was just like holding this little book and just feeling and thinking about how powerful objects are. The thing about material and stuff. We live in a material world, we think. And if we look deeply into any object there's just such gravity to it, you know. It's amazing. How could this book be here? Created by these people expressing something in my hands now.

The feeling of it, the weight of it, the existence of it. And maybe the uniqueness and surprise of this particular book helped me to experience this feeling of amazement. This feeling of connection. Maybe that's easier for my habitual mind mode than if it was just another trade paperback from Shambhala Press. Hundreds of those. Maybe there are only ten of these in the world. We don't know. There's a sort of bottomless kind of somethingness to everything. A kind of is-ness. Somehow this little book reminded me of that. That this is. That this little book is. That we are. That this place is. That the sun came up and went down. That all of this is. It's incredible. And of course everything is that way.
